speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) how will the US-China Phase 1 Trade Deal impact Singapore's economy; and (b) how can local manufacturers that export parts for US goods leverage the new agreement to boost their businesses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will group the answers into two parts: first, global developments and their potential impact on Singapore's economy; second, the Government's strategies to grow Singapore's economy and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Twenty-nineteen was a volatile year for the global economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fortunately, the global economy avoided several worse scenarios, including an all-out trade war between the United States (US) and China, but downside risks remain.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a small, open economy, Singapore was affected by these macroeconomic conditions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our non-oil domestic exports declined by 10.1% on a year-on-year basis between January and November 2019.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Even though we are cautiously optimistic, there remains several uncertainties in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The biggest uncertainty is the relationship between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the most important bilateral relationship for both countries, and indeed for the entire world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We welcome the announcement of the Phase 1 trade deal, especially the cancellation of further tariff hikes in December 2019.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Averting further trade tensions is positive news for all countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We hope that this is the first step towards putting the relationship back on a stronger footing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We look forward to learning about the details of the Phase 1 deal on 15 January 2020 and working with both countries to grow our economies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another uncertainty pertains to Brexit, for the United Kingdom (UK) and the European Union (EU) are collectively our third largest trading partner in goods, and our biggest trading partners in services.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng had filed a Parliamentary Question for the next Sitting on the implications of Brexit on Singapore and Singaporean companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Based on the terms of the draft Withdrawal Agreement, the immediate impact of Brexit is likely to be limited.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is because, until 31 December 2020 at the least, the UK will functionally be treated as an EU member state and remain a party to the EU's international agreements, including the EU-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (EUSFTA) which had just come into force.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, this may change depending on what the UK Parliament decides in these coming weeks.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In addition, what happens after 2020 has not yet been determined.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singapore is, therefore, working with the UK on an economic agreement to maintain continuity in our economic relations after the EUSFTA no longer applies to the UK.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I wish to remind Members that these uncertainties are not unrelated.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What is happening between the US and China, the UK and the EU, and other economies like India, Chile and Hong Kong, are manifestations of a deeper unhappiness over the inequitable distribution of gains from globalisation, and a concern that tomorrow will not be better than today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why the multilateral trading system, which has underpinned decades of economic integration and free trade, is itself under significant stress.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Since 11 December 2019, the World Trade Organization's (WTO's) Appellate Body has been non-functional because there are not enough appellate judges to meet the quorum.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The WTO's appellate function is an existential one for the multilateral trading system, because it ensures the robust enforcement of multilateral trade rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Without this binding and neutral mechanism to resolve trade disputes, the risk of a fragmented trading system will grow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There will be severe consequences for all WTO members, including Singapore, should trade, talent and data flows become disrupted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The strategic question confronting the world is whether we continue to turn inward and less open, or we find a new balance that enables economies to remain open and connected, while ensuring that our people benefit equitably from such integration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Apart from these challenges, there are also unanticipated issues that may affect the global economy, such as the situation between the US and Iran.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Any escalation between the two countries may portend further instability in the Middle East which could have negative implications on the global economy, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I should add that this is not all doom and gloom for the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are also many exciting opportunities to harness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, the digital economy is a major opportunity for us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Digitalisation enables small countries like Singapore to transcend our size and geography and helps our enterprises to penetrate new regional and global markets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Within Southeast Asia alone, the digital market is estimated to exceed US$300 billion by 2025, almost the same size as the current Singapore economy and right at our doorsteps!

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And although the IMF has downgraded the global growth forecasts, Asia remains a bright spot with growth estimated at 5.1%.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In sum, there will be both uncertainties and opportunities in the year ahead.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is incumbent on us to ensure our ship is seaworthy, set our sails to catch the wind.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government will help Singapore businesses navigate the challenges and seize the opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This includes helping Singaporean companies to expand into overseas markets, as well as providing customised support for companies to press on with productivity improvements, innovation and the training of our workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singapore has to adopt a long-term perspective in our economic strategies, even as we tackle the short-term headwinds.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Allow me to elaborate on three strategies that the Government has taken to grow our economy and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, we are strengthening Singapore's fundamentals to distinguish ourselves amidst the uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In July last year, I shared with Members some of the factors that have enabled Singapore to stand out from the competition.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These investments are in high value-added sectors, such as electronics, aerospace and pharmaceuticals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have not included investments from other sectors in the above figure, such as the $9 billion expansion plan for the two integrated resorts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These investments will create many good jobs for Singaporeans, and they reflect the global business community's confidence in our future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Moving forward, we will continue to deepen our linkages with key markets and transcend our geographical boundaries by pushing into new dimensions of connectivity that include the flows of data, talent, ideas and technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, we are helping Singapore companies and workers to internationalise and turn the world into our hinterland.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The preconditions are in place, thanks to our excellent connectivity and our extensive network of 25 Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) with 64 trading partners, which collectively account for more than 85% of global GDP and more than 90% of Singapore's trade.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the same period, about 1,700 companies were supported in growing their businesses both domestically and overseas through the Enterprise Development Grant (EDG) programme in the areas of capability development, market access and manpower development for internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These transformation efforts have translated into higher pay and better career progression opportunities for our workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As businesses grow, they will create more good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These outcomes may include wage increases, job creation, job redesign or hiring of older workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will reinforce our message of building an economy that is both pro-enterprise and pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Besides EDG, there are also employee-specific schemes like the Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) to help mid-career professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) reskill and embark on new careers, and the Global Ready Talent (GRT) programme to equip workers with skills relating to internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through these programmes, we hope to prepare more Singaporeans to compete and succeed across the region and in the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government will announce further initiatives to help our businesses transform and build stronger capabilities at this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through the work of the Future Economy Council (FEC) and the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs), we are developing new industry niches in areas, such as additive manufacturing, robotics and sensors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These build on our existing strengths in sectors, such as electronics and precision engineering, and will enhance Singapore's position in the global value chains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are also partnering industry players to develop new capabilities in promising growth areas, such as agri-food, urban mobility and precision medicine.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, we will be establishing the Agri-Food Innovation Park (AFIP) in Sungei Kadut, to bring together high-tech farming and research and development activities in areas, such as urban agriculture and aquaculture.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through this, we hope to create new career opportunities and grow a new generation of technopreneur farmers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To capture opportunities in the digital economy, Singapore is co-leading the WTO Joint Statement Initiative on E-Commerce (JSI).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: JSI will establish multilateral rules to help companies navigate the complex e-commerce landscape.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are exploring deeper collaborations with key economic partners like Chile, Australia and New Zealand through a new generation of "digital economy agreements" to open up more opportunities for our companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But there are steps that we can take to strengthen our economic competitiveness and build stronger capabilities in our enterprises and workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our success has always been predicated on our will to make the best of what we have, and our resolve to turn adversity into opportunity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we continue to stay united and work together as one people, we can all look forward to a brighter tomorrow for all of us.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One, can the Minister share, in his view or MTI's view, whether the US-China tensions will continue to ease off in 2020 and whether it will still continue in terms of the tensed landscape as well as what its impact will be on Singapore companies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, the Minister mentioned about multilateral agreements that will continue to be beneficial for the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share with the House about the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), whether there are any developments on that front and how Singapore is playing on that front and whether Singapore can benefit?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are encouraged by the conclusion and the impending signing of the Phase 1 agreement between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have spoken to both my counterparts in the US and China.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think the significance of the deal goes beyond just the lines of agreement and the specific line items in the agreement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think both the US and China are very clear that this is a basis for them to establish the strategic trust between both countries because a deal is a deal.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: More important is how we implement the deal and, along the way, there will be further negotiations between them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we are cheered by the conclusion of Phase 1.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But having said that, we are very clear – and I think both the US and China are also very clear – that the challenges between the two countries go beyond the trade numbers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They have differences between themselves; how they see they should structure their economies in terms of subsidies; they have differences in how they see trade relationships; they have differences in how they see the subsidies for their technology, research and development, so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, there are deeper structural issues that have to be settled between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think that we will have to wait for the strategic trust to be built up for them to move on to the next step of their agreement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Given the political dynamics in the US in 2020, we can also expect some surprises along the way.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, while we are cautiously optimistic, we are cheered by the trade, the Phase 1 trade deal, I think there are many other issues that still need to be resolved in time to come between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are a few outstanding bilateral market access negotiations between some of the RCEP countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, the legal scrubbing for the text have commenced and our team is currently now in Jakarta working with our counterparts on that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think every one of the 15 member states would welcome India's continued participation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have continued to keep India in the loop for all the discussions and also the legal scrubbing.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: There has been a request to take Question Nos 3 and 4 together, so Minister for Manpower will answer Question No 3 and the Minister for Trade and Industry, Question No 4.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And we will take the supplementary questions immediately after the response to Question No 4.
